title: State v. Archna Shukla
court: Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
result: Owner Archna Shukla convicted u/s 135 r/w 150 (abetment); user/tenant Amit absconding (not arrested); civil liability (theft bill Rs. 56506) settled and deposited with NOC issued; posted for sentence

interpretations.interpretation: A two-core black aluminium cable tapped directly from the licensee's LV mains (Section 135(1)(a)).
'Consumer' includes the owner/registered consumer, not only the actual user; the owner is answerable for illegal abstraction found at the premises even where a tenant is the user (Lokesh Chandela).

A registered consumer/owner who consciously permits a tenant to draw an unauthorised supply abets the theft and is punishable u/s 150 with the principal's punishment. NEW: the abettor-owner can be convicted even though the actual user/principal has absconded and is never arrested or tried — the abettor's liability is independent of the principal being in the dock.

Compulsory presumption on proof of an unauthorised means (Neeraj Dutt) rebuttable on the prudent-man standard (Hiten P. Dalal); the owner-abettor must show lawful metered use / paid bills (s.106; Mukesh Rastogi).

citations.case: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashwani Kumar
citations.principle: An inspection report prepared by officers in discharge of official duty carries a presumption of regularity; onus on the consumer to rebut by cogent evidence.

citations.case: Sushil Sharma v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Non-examination of an independent/public witness is no infirmity where inspecting officials are trustworthy and bear no enmity to the accused.

citations.case: Lokesh Chandela v. State of NCT & Ors.
citations.principle: Both user and owner/registered consumer fall within 'consumer' under Section 2(15); registered consumer answerable for illegal abstraction found at the premises.
'Shall presume' denotes a compulsory legal presumption the court is bound to draw until the fact is disproved.

citations.case: Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee
citations.principle: Rebuttal of a statutory presumption need not be conclusive; evidence must make the defence reasonably probable to a prudent man.

citations.case: Mukesh Rastogi v. North Delhi Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Easiest rebuttal of the theft presumption is production of paid electricity bills; Section 106 Evidence Act places that onus on the consumer.

significance.point: An owner can be convicted of abetment even where the user has absconded
significance.explanation: The registered consumer/owner who consciously permits an unarrested, untried tenant to draw an unauthorised supply is guilty u/s 135 r/w 150; the principal's absence from the dock does not absolve the abettor.
The owner cannot disown liability for illegal abstraction at the premises merely because a tenant was the user (Lokesh Chandela).

significance.point: The reverse-onus presumption binds the owner-abettor
significance.explanation: Once the unauthorised means is proved, the owner must show lawful metered use — paid bills (s.106; Mukesh Rastogi) — failing which the compulsory presumption convicts.

significance.point: Settlement, deposit and even an NOC are not immunity
significance.explanation: Closing the civil account does not answer the s.135 charge; the settlement is read as conduct corroborating the theft.

significance.point: A public witness is not essential
significance.explanation: Official inspection testimony suffices absent shown enmity (Ashwani Kumar; Sushil Sharma).
